nameStory: This little plant earned its name "chickweed" because chickens absolutely love to eat it! Farmers have long noticed their feathered friends eagerly pecking at these tender green plants, which are packed with nutrition. The scientific name Stellaria means "little star," referring to the tiny white star-shaped flowers that dot the plant.
description: Common chickweed is a low-growing annual plant that forms sprawling mats across the ground. It has small, oval leaves that grow opposite each other on weak, trailing stems that rarely get taller than a few inches. The plant produces tiny white flowers with five deeply notched petals that look like ten narrow petals at first glance. This humble little plant is actually quite hardy, growing almost year-round in mild weather.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white star-shaped flowers about 1/4 inch across with five deeply split petals that appear as ten narrow white strips. The flowers feel delicate and papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. They feel soft and succulent when you rub them between your fingers, with a fresh, mild taste if you nibble them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, sprawling mats that hug the ground, with weak stems that trail and root at joints where they touch soil. The whole plant feels tender and breaks easily when pulled.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctive line of fine white hairs running down one side of the round, pale green stem - this stripe of fuzz switches sides at each leaf joint, creating a zigzag pattern.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny brown seeds develop in small capsules that split open when ripe, releasing seeds that feel like fine grit when rubbed between fingers.

habitat: Chickweed thrives in disturbed, fertile soils throughout New England, from gardens and lawns to farm fields and waste areas. You'll find it in both sunny and partially shaded spots, especially where the soil stays moist and rich in nutrients. It's particularly common around homes, along paths, and anywhere humans have disturbed the natural vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Fresh green growth emerges early, often while snow still lingers. Small white flowers begin appearing in late spring, and the plant starts its rapid spreading growth.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering and producing seeds throughout the warm months, though growth may slow during hot, dry periods. Plants stay low and mat-like.
seasonality.fall: Often experiences a second flush of vigorous growth as cool weather returns. Seeds mature and disperse, while plants may stay green well into late fall.
seasonality.winter: In mild winters, chickweed can stay green and even continue growing slowly. In harsh cold, plants die back but seeds remain dormant in soil until spring.

funFact: Chickweed is nature's own refrigerator thermometer - it only opens its tiny white flowers when the temperature is above 60°F, and the flowers actually close up tight on chilly or cloudy days, making it a surprisingly accurate weather predictor!
confusionNotes: Mouse-ear chickweed (which is fuzzy all over) is the most common look-alike, but common chickweed's distinctive single line of hairs on the stem is the dead giveaway. Remember: "Common chickweed has a hairy highway" - that single stripe of fuzz running down one side of the stem.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name "weed" fool you - this plant is completely edible and has been used as food and medicine for thousands of years. Many gardeners actually appreciate chickweed as a living mulch that protects soil and provides fresh greens, though others consider it a persistent garden pest.
compareHints: Among its Stellaria relatives in New England, common chickweed is the only one with that telltale single line of hairs on the stem - other chickweeds and stitchworts are either hairless or fuzzy all over. It's also the most robust and mat-forming of the group, while most of its cousins like lesser stitchwort grow more upright with narrower, grassier leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Lesser stitchwort differs from common chickweed by having much narrower, grass-like leaves instead of oval ones, and deeply notched petals that create a clear star shape rather than chickweed's more rounded appearance.
Among the chickweeds and stitchworts in New England, water chickweed stands out for its wet habitat preferences and larger size.
Among New England's chickweeds and starworts, boreal starwort is distinguished by its four-angled stems and deeply-lobed petals that create pronounced star shapes.
Star chickweed stands out from other chickweeds by preferring woodland habitats over disturbed areas, and having much larger, more showy flowers than its weedy relatives.
Unlike the common chickweed found in gardens and lawns, bog stitchwort is strictly a wetland specialist with much narrower leaves.
Among New England's starworts and chickweeds, long-leaved starwort stands out for its exceptionally narrow, grass-like leaves and preference for consistently wet habitats.
Wood stitchwort differs from its chickweed cousins mainly in its deeper petal notches and preference for consistently moist woodland soils.
Lesser chickweed differs from common chickweed by typically lacking flowers entirely and being much smaller in all dimensions.
